question: What is the purpose of @BeforeEach and @AfterEach in JUnit 5?
title: @BeforeEach @AfterEach JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **`@BeforeEach`** and **`@AfterEach`** are lifecycle hooks that run around each Jupiter test invocation. Use them to create the fixture needed by that test and release per-test resources. They support isolation, but only the code inside the hooks resets external or static state. Dynamic tests created by one `@TestFactory` do not each receive a separate before/after-each cycle.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`@BeforeEach` / `@AfterEach`** — run around each Jupiter test invocation.
- **Isolation support** — put explicit fixture creation and cleanup in the hooks; they do not reset external state automatically.
- **Default instance lifecycle** — `PER_METHOD` creates a new test object per test method or invocation.
- **Cleanup** — `@AfterEach` is invoked after a test failure, though process termination or a failure in setup can still affect cleanup guarantees.
- **Class-level hooks** — `@BeforeAll`/`@AfterAll` run once for the container and are normally static under `PER_METHOD`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`@BeforeEach` and `@AfterEach` are lifecycle hooks around each Jupiter test invocation. I use the before hook to create the fixture that several tests share and the after hook to release per-test resources. For a shopping cart, the before hook can create an empty cart before each test.

Under the default `PER_METHOD` lifecycle, JUnit creates a new test-class instance for each test method or invocation. That isolates ordinary instance fields, but static fields, a database, files, and remote systems are still shared unless the test resets or isolates them. `@AfterEach` is invoked after a failed test, so it is the right lifecycle location for cleanup, although process termination and setup failures can still affect what cleanup is possible.

`@BeforeAll` and `@AfterAll` run once for the container. Under `PER_METHOD` they are normally static; `PER_CLASS` permits instance methods. Choose each versus all by resource scope, not only by setup cost.

sections.title: Fresh setup surrounds every test invocation
sections.content:
**`@BeforeEach`** runs before every test invocation and prepares a clean fixture. **`@AfterEach`** runs afterward and releases per-test resources. This surrounding lifecycle also applies to each row of a parameterized test.

For example, `@BeforeEach` can create a new in-memory cart so one test’s items never appear in another test. `@AfterEach` can close a temporary server or clear a resource that the test opened. Expensive resources shared by the whole class belong in `@BeforeAll` and `@AfterAll`, not in per-test hooks. Setup should remain visible enough that a reader understands the scenario; hiding all inputs in a large `@BeforeEach` makes tests harder to read and can conceal unwanted shared assumptions.

sections.title: Per-Test Lifecycle
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["new test instance"] --> B["@BeforeEach
build fresh state"] B --> C["@Test
run one test"] C --> D["@AfterEach
clean up resources"] D --> E["repeat for
next test"] ```

sections.title: Fresh State Before Each Test
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing Each with All.** `@BeforeEach` runs per test; `@BeforeAll` runs once. Heavy setup in `@BeforeEach` slows the suite, but shared mutable setup in `@BeforeAll` breaks isolation.
- **Relying on leftover state.** Expecting a field populated by a previous test — fragile and order-dependent. Build state in `@BeforeEach`.
- **Cleanup in the test body.** If the test fails before cleanup, resources leak. Put cleanup in `@AfterEach`.
- **Using JUnit 4 names.** It's `@BeforeEach`/`@AfterEach`, not `@Before`/`@After`.

question: What does @DisplayName do in JUnit 5 and why should you use it?
title: @DisplayName JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **`@DisplayName`** gives a test method or class a **human-readable name** shown in IDEs, Maven Surefire reports, and CI dashboards instead of the raw method name. It can contain spaces, punctuation, even emoji, so reports read like specifications — `@DisplayName("rejects withdrawal above balance")`. It's documentation that doesn't change behavior.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`@DisplayName`** = free-form readable label for a test or class.
- **Shows** in IDEs, Surefire reports, and CI dashboards.
- **No behavior change** — purely cosmetic.
- **Pairs with `@Nested`** so reports read as full sentences.
- **Keep method names good too** — code readers don't see display names.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
DisplayName gives a test or a test class a human-readable name that shows up in the IDE, in the Maven Surefire report, and on CI dashboards, instead of the raw Java method name. Method names have to follow Java identifier rules, so they end up camel-cased and a bit awkward to read. A display name is just a free-form string, so it can have spaces and punctuation. That means a report can say rejects a withdrawal larger than the balance, which reads like a specification, instead of the squished method name.

The key thing to understand is that it's purely cosmetic. It doesn't affect which tests are discovered, the order they run in, or whether they run at all — it only changes the label in reports. So it's really a documentation feature.

Where it shines is combined with the Nested annotation. If I have a nested class with a display name and tests with display names, the report reads as a full sentence — something like BankAccount, when empty, rejects a withdrawal. That's genuinely useful when a non-engineer, like a QA lead or a product owner, is looking at the CI output.

Common mistakes are letting the method names get sloppy because I'm relying on display names — teammates still read the method names in the source — and writing vague display names like test one, which throws away the benefit.

sections.title: Display names improve reports without changing execution
sections.content:
**`@DisplayName`** assigns a free-form label to a test class or method. JUnit uses that label in test trees and reports, but it does not change discovery, execution order, or test behavior. The Java method name still matters to people reading and navigating the source.

For example, `@DisplayName("rejects a withdrawal above the balance")` gives a failure a plain-language label. Combined with an outer or `@Nested` class display name such as “when the account is empty,” the report reads as a meaningful scenario. A display name should describe behavior, not repeat a vague label such as “test 1.” It is documentation for results, not a replacement for clear method and class names.

sections.title: @DisplayName at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|What it is|~Readable test label|free-form string|spaces & punctuation OK|shows in reports/IDE
blue|Where it shows|~Report surfaces|IDE test tree|Surefire HTML|CI dashboards
amber|What it isn't|~No behavior change|doesn't affect discovery|not a method-name replacement|keep names good too
violet|Best with|~Pairs nicely|@Nested groups|reads as sentences|business-readable output

sections.title: Display Names That Read Like Specs
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Letting method names rot.** `@DisplayName` is for reports; teammates still read method names in code. Keep both descriptive.
- **Expecting behavior changes.** It doesn't change discovery, order, or whether a test runs.
- **Vague display names.** `@DisplayName("test 1")` wastes the feature; describe the scenario.
- **Overusing emoji.** Fun, but can render badly in some CI logs — keep it readable.

question: What is @ExtendWith in JUnit 5 and when do you use it?
title: @ExtendWith JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **`@ExtendWith`** registers a JUnit Jupiter extension. An extension can provide lifecycle callbacks, parameter resolution, exception handling, or test-instance processing. **`MockitoExtension`** initializes Mockito annotations and applies Mockito's strictness rules; **`SpringExtension`** connects Jupiter to Spring's TestContext framework, whose other annotations decide which context is loaded. Multiple extensions can be registered, unlike JUnit 4's one-runner model.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`@ExtendWith`** registers a Jupiter extension.
- **`MockitoExtension`** initializes `@Mock`/`@InjectMocks` and applies Mockito lifecycle rules.
- **`SpringExtension`** integrates Spring's TestContext framework; context configuration comes from Spring test annotations.
- **Composable** — multiple extensions can be registered, unlike JUnit 4's single `@RunWith` runner.
- **Spring Boot tests** — annotations such as `@SpringBootTest`, `@WebMvcTest`, and `@DataJpaTest` already carry Spring's extension support.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
ExtendWith is how I register an extension in JUnit 5, and an extension is basically a plugin that hooks into the test lifecycle. It can run code before and after tests, resolve parameters, or post-process the test instance. I just point ExtendWith at the extension class and JUnit wires it in.

The two I use all the time are the Mockito extension and the Spring extension. The Mockito extension initializes my Mock and InjectMocks fields and also reports unnecessary stubbing, which catches mistakes. The Spring extension boots up the Spring application context so I can autowire beans in a test.

The history here matters. In JUnit 4 you used RunWith, and the big limitation was that you could only have one runner per class. So you had to choose between, say, the Mockito runner and the Spring runner. JUnit 5 replaced that with the extension model, and the key improvement is that it's composable — I can stack multiple extensions on the same class. That's a real practical win.

The most common fresher mistake is still using RunWith with JUnit 5, in which case it's just ignored and your Mock fields come back null, so you get a NullPointerException on the first stub. The fix is ExtendWith with the Mockito extension. Another subtle point is that you don't add the Spring extension manually when you're already using SpringBootTest or WebMvcTest, because those meta-annotations already include it.

sections.title: Extensions connect tools to the JUnit lifecycle
sections.content:
**`@ExtendWith`** registers one or more JUnit Jupiter extensions. An extension can take part in discovery, create or resolve parameters, run setup and cleanup callbacks, or react to test results. This is the JUnit 5 replacement for many jobs previously handled by JUnit 4 runners and rules.

For example, `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` initializes `@Mock` fields and resolves Mockito’s test lifecycle. Spring’s testing support uses `SpringExtension` to connect the TestContext framework. Multiple extensions can be declared because the extension model is composable; a JUnit 4 class could have only one `@RunWith` runner. Register only extensions the test needs, because an extension can add setup cost or alter lifecycle behavior.

sections.title: @ExtendWith at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|What it is|~Registers an extension|lifecycle callbacks|parameter resolution|test-instance processing
blue|MockitoExtension|~Initializes Mockito|@Mock and @InjectMocks|strictness rules|Jupiter integration
amber|SpringExtension|~Connects TestContext|supports dependency injection|context chosen by Spring annotations|included in Boot test annotations
violet|vs @RunWith|~JUnit 4 -> Jupiter|one runner in JUnit 4|multiple extensions|composable model

sections.title: JUnit 4: a single @RunWith runner
JUnit 5: @ExtendWith, stackable
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Mixing JUnit 4 and Jupiter models.** `@RunWith` belongs to JUnit 4; Jupiter uses `@ExtendWith`. A JUnit 4 test can still run through the Vintage engine, so check imports and engine configuration rather than assuming it is ignored.
- **Forgetting Mockito initialization.** `@Mock` fields need `MockitoExtension` or a correctly managed `openMocks` call.
- **Re-adding SpringExtension.** `@SpringBootTest`, `@WebMvcTest`, and `@DataJpaTest` already include it.
- **Mixing Mockito initialization styles.** Choose the extension or `MockitoAnnotations.openMocks`, and close the latter's returned handle.

question: What is @Nested in JUnit 5 and how does it improve test organization?
title: @Nested Tests JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **`@Nested`** groups related tests in an **inner, non-static class** so the report reads like an outline — grouping a unit's tests by state or scenario (e.g. `WhenEmpty`, `WhenFunded`). Outer `@BeforeEach` runs before the nested class's `@BeforeEach`, letting you layer setup from general to specific. It improves readability and makes failures self-locating.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`@Nested`** = inner non-static class grouping a scenario.
- **Layered setup** — outer `@BeforeEach` before inner `@BeforeEach`.
- **Non-static required** — static breaks it.
- **Pair with `@DisplayName`** for sentence-like reports.
- **Same unit only** — split unrelated units into separate classes.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`@Nested` marks a non-static inner class as a group of related tests. A bank-account test can have `WhenEmpty` and `WhenFunded` groups, so the report shows the state in which a failure occurred.

Setup is layered. The outer `@BeforeEach` runs before the nested class's `@BeforeEach`, allowing common setup first and scenario-specific setup second. For example, the outer hook creates a new account and the funded group's hook deposits money.

The nested test class itself must be non-static. An instance `@BeforeAll` inside it needs `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)`; on Java versions that permit static members in inner classes, a static callback is also possible. Use enough nesting to clarify scenarios, but stop when the setup becomes hard to trace.

sections.title: Nested classes build a scenario tree
sections.content:
**`@Nested`** turns a non-static inner class into a group of tests within the outer test class. It is meant for related states of the same unit, so both the source and the test report can read from general context to specific behavior.

For example, `BankAccountTest` can contain `WhenEmpty` and `WhenFunded` nested classes. The outer `@BeforeEach` creates a fresh account, then the funded group’s own `@BeforeEach` deposits money before each test in that group. Outer setup runs before inner setup, allowing context to be layered without copy-and-paste. Avoid deep nesting and do not use nested classes to combine unrelated production classes; separate units still belong in separate top-level test classes.

sections.title: @Nested at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|What it is|~Inner non-static class|sub-scenario group|outline-style report|same unit, many states
blue|Lifecycle|~Layered setup|outer @BeforeEach first|then inner @BeforeEach|general to specific
amber|Class callbacks|~Follow lifecycle rules|instance @BeforeAll needs PER_CLASS|static callback depends on Java level|avoid hidden shared state
violet|Pairs with|~@DisplayName|sentence-like reports|self-locating failures|business-readable

sections.title: Scenario Grouping with Layered Setup
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Static nested class.** A Jupiter `@Nested` test class must be non-static.
- **Instance `@BeforeAll` without `PER_CLASS`.** Add `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)` when the callback needs the nested instance; a static callback is another option where the Java language level permits it.
- **Over-nesting.** Deep layers make setup and reports harder to follow.
- **Grouping unrelated units.** Different production units normally belong in separate top-level test classes.
